name: Yogurt (live-culture or probiotic; eaten in most studies)
short: Yogurt-linked outbreaks: botulism deaths; haemolytic uraemic syndrome in 5 children. Rare blood/heart infections, mostly in the ill. Milk-allergic children may react. Pregnancy: mixed data.
text: This entry covers yogurt and fermented milk eaten or drunk; one pregnancy trial does not state the route, and one trial in a cited review used yogurt in the vagina. Infections (case reports): an elderly man with heart disease and diabetes developed Lactobacillus rhamnosus bloodstream infection and endocarditis after eating large amounts of Greek yogurt and later died after a heart attack and cardiac arrest; septic shock from a yogurt-derived Lactobacillus strain occurred in a man after high-dose chemotherapy and stem cell transplantation, and bloodstream infections linked to yogurt are reported in a patient with Crohn's disease and HIV who was taking ustekinumab, in a patient with AIDS, and in a toddler with intestinal failure who had a central venous catheter; a Lactococcus lactis liver abscess was linked to live-culture yogurt in an adult with a normal immune system. A young man who ate large quantities of probiotic yogurt developed Lactobacillus rhamnosus endocarditis and septic arthritis; the report's title asks whether the yogurt was the cause, and routine laboratory methods could not tell the infecting bacterium from the yogurt's bacteria, but more appropriate methods, including PCR, distinguished it from the yogurt isolate; the abstract describes no underlying illness. A man with a weakened immune system developed rhinocerebral mucormycosis after eating yogurt that was found to be contaminated with the mould Mucor circinelloides. Contamination outbreaks (outbreak reports): in north-west England from September to November 1991, 16 people had verotoxin-producing E. coli O157 infection, which a case-control study linked to eating a locally produced live yoghurt (the abstract reports an association and does not say the organism was found in the yoghurt); 11 of them were aged 10 or under, and 5 of these children developed haemolytic uraemic syndrome. In the UK's largest recorded outbreak of foodborne botulism, in June 1989, 27 people fell ill and one died; 25 of them had eaten one brand of hazelnut yoghurt, which contained a hazelnut conserve; botulinum toxin was found in a can of the conserve and in cartons of the yoghurt, and the processing of the conserve was judged inadequate to destroy the spores. In a family outbreak in eastern Anatolia, Turkey, in late September 2005, a teenage boy and his mother died of botulism and 8 more cases, with milder symptoms, were identified later and recovered; the source was condensed yoghurt that had been buried under soil, in which type A botulinum toxin was found. In an outbreak, more than 200 consumers became ill with nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea after commercial yogurts contaminated with Mucor circinelloides were sold (the abstract gives no date and does not say whether this was the same contamination as in the mucormycosis case above). A 2011 review of probiotic safety in general (yogurt was one delivery vehicle) found no increased risk of adverse events in randomised trials, which did not routinely monitor for the bloodstream infections described in case studies, while case studies suggested that people in compromised health are most likely to have adverse events. Milk allergy: in children with cow's milk allergy given a yogurt challenge, 17 of 34 reacted in one study, and 15 of 16 children with IgE-mediated allergy who reacted to unheated milk also reacted to yogurt in another; a 5-month-old girl developed vomiting, cough and diarrhoea after yogurt, diagnosed as a milk-protein enterocolitis syndrome. Trials: in 70 children aged 1 to 12 taking antibiotics, those given a probiotic yogurt reported fewer adverse events than those given pasteurised yogurt (abdominal pain, vomiting and headache in one child each, against abdominal pain in 6, loss of appetite in 4 and nausea in 1); in meta-analyses of fermented milk added to Helicobacter pylori treatment, side effects were not significantly changed (odds ratio 0.51 and risk ratio 0.71, both not significant); 21 adults with HIV given yogurts supplemented with micronutrients, probiotics or both reported no adverse events. The meta-analysis of yogurt for acute gastroenteritis in children in hospital reports no safety data. Pregnancy: in an open-label trial of 310 pregnant women with bacterial vaginosis in the third trimester, preterm birth occurred in 12 women given probiotic yogurt and 7 given clindamycin by mouth (no test reported), and prelabour rupture of membranes in 9 and 5 (not significant); the abstract does not say whether the yogurt was eaten. In a randomised trial in 130 overweight or obese pregnant women without diabetes who ate probiotic or conventional yoghurt from 24 weeks of pregnancy until delivery, one woman in each group had a foetal death in the womb, and preterm deliveries (3 and 8) and other maternal and infant outcomes did not differ significantly between the groups. A Cochrane review found insufficient trial data to assess the effect of probiotics on preterm birth; of its two trials, one used fermented milk by mouth and one used yogurt put in the vagina. No interaction data were found in the cited sources; two of the infection cases were in people taking ustekinumab or after high-dose chemotherapy.
